name: Maxilla expansion for forward growth (face pulling/reverse-pull headgear)

lead: Reverse-pull headgear, also called a facemask or face pulling device, is an orthodontic appliance used to bring the upper jaw and midface forward for better midface support and profile. It is used in children with underbites and a recessed upper jaw.

A frame rests on the forehead and chin, with elastics attached to the teeth to pull the upper jaw forward, often after rapid palatal expansion. Orthodontic literature reports that treatment in the deciduous and mixed dentition can produce forward skeletal movement of the maxilla through remodeling of the sutures around it, often with dentoalveolar effects. Forum users discuss it as a midface tool, though the evidence concerns growing children.

paras: An orthodontist fits the appliance and sets the elastics, and it is worn for set hours over months, typically in childhood when the sutures are still responsive. It is commonly paired with palatal expansion.
Dentoalveolar side effects are reported, and long-term follow-up shows some patients relapse. Use is guided by an orthodontist, and the evidence applies to growing children, not adults.

angle.text: Forum users discuss reverse-pull headgear, or face pulling, as a way to bring the upper jaw and midface forward for better support and profile. It has been studied in children with underbites and a recessed upper jaw; use as an adult appearance tool is based on user reports.

lead: Reverse-pull headgear, also called a facemask or protraction facemask, is an orthodontic appliance with a frame in front of the face that rests on the forehead and chin, with elastics attached to the teeth or an intraoral appliance to pull the upper jaw (maxilla) forward and downward.[1] Orthodontists prescribe it for children with Class III malocclusion and a retrusive maxilla, where the upper jaw sits behind the lower, and it is often combined with rapid palatal expansion.[2][3] The goal is a more forward-set midface and an upper jaw that meets the lower jaw correctly, which changes both the bite and the facial profile.

Orthodontic literature reports that treatment in the deciduous and mixed dentition can produce skeletal forward movement of the maxilla through remodeling of the circummaxillary sutures, though it is often accompanied by dentoalveolar effects such as tooth movement, and long-term follow-up shows that some patients relapse.[4][2][5][6] Newer bone-anchored techniques, in which elastics attach to miniplates screwed to the bone rather than to teeth, aim to deliver skeletal change with fewer tooth effects, and recent systematic reviews have compared them with the conventional facemask.[4][7][7]

In appearance communities the same idea is discussed as 'face pulling': pulling the maxilla forward with the thumbs or an improvised or purchased headgear in the hope of improving midface projection. The published evidence concerns growing children treated by orthodontists under supervision; no study has examined thumb pulling, or facemask use for appearance, in adults.[8][9]
infobox: Protraction facemask, orthopedic facemask, reverse-pull headgear[1]
Growing children with maxillary deficiency (Class III)[2]
Early intervention typically ages 7 to 13 per Wikipedia; starting before age 8 is recommended in the literature[2][10]
12 to 23 hours daily; 14 to 16 hours typical[10]
Bone-anchored protraction with miniplates; orthognathic surgery after growth[4][14]

paras: A facemask pulls forward and downward on the upper jaw, the opposite direction of conventional headgear, which is why it is called reverse-pull.[1] It is paired with rapid palatal expansion in many protocols, which is thought to loosen the sutures so the maxilla can respond to the forward force.[2] Wikipedia notes that the appliance effectively pulls the teeth forward, which is why orthodontic studies track both skeletal and dental change.[10]

Angle's 1899 classification describes Class III (mesiocclusion) as a bite in which the upper molar sits behind its normal position, often with the lower front teeth more prominent.[3] The skeletal pattern can be mandibular prognathism, maxillary retrognathism or a combination, and Wikipedia reports that Class III affects 3 to 8 percent of the UK population, with higher incidence reported in Asia.[3] Treatment options listed include growth modification, orthodontic camouflage for mild discrepancies, and orthognathic surgery such as bilateral sagittal split osteotomy for horizontal mandibular excess.[3] The facemask is aimed at the maxillary-deficiency form, in children who are still growing.

Wikipedia describes the orthodontic facemask as having three parts: a face frame stabilized by a forehead pad and a chin cup, sometimes with a head cap whose straps hold the frame in place, and elastics that run from a horizontal bar in front of the mouth to braces or an appliance in the mouth.[1] Up to six elastics may supply forward and sideways forces while the child can still open and close the jaw.[1]

Wikipedia gives the range of wear as 12 to 23 hours a day, with 14 to 16 hours typical, and overall treatment of 12 to 18 months depending on the severity of the bite and growth.[10] Children and adolescents generally adapt within a few weeks, and because daytime wear is hard to maintain, appliances are mostly worn in the evening and during sleep.[10]

Rapid palatal (maxillary) expansion uses a screw-driven appliance to widen the upper jaw, and in facemask protocols it is used to disturb the sutures before or alongside protraction.[2][11] Wikipedia traces palatal expansion to Westcott's 1859 report of mechanical force on the maxilla and Emerson Angell's 1860 paper, with the Haas expander reintroduced in the US in 1956.[11] Expansion is most common between ages 8 and 18; after puberty the palatal halves fuse, so expansion typically requires mini-implant-supported (MARPE) or surgically assisted (SARPE) approaches, and expansion after the growth spurt causes more dental tipping than skeletal change.[11] Common side effects include speech difficulty, excess saliva, a gap between the upper front teeth, and relapse, with studies cited by Wikipedia finding that one third to one half of the expansion can be lost before it stabilizes.[11]

The literature has recommended starting before age 8, though a 1997 study stated that this had not been supported by scientific data and examined patients both younger and older than 8.[2] A 2000 study of 60 Japanese children in mixed dentition examined whether bone age helps plan treatment timing.[6] Wikipedia notes that early intervention, typically between ages 7 and 13, is often recommended by parents and doctors as a way of avoiding later surgery.[10] The common thread is that these studies treat children whose sutures are still responsive.

A 1997 study compared children younger and older than 8 years treated with reverse-pull headgear and rapid palatal expansion, to test the recommendation to start before age 8.[2] A 2000 study of 60 Japanese children in mixed dentition measured cephalometric change over one year and described the main skeletal effect as forward movement of the maxilla through remodeling of the circummaxillary sutures.[6] The 2006 Angle Orthodontist follow-up evaluated cephalometric radiographs of 41 Class III children before and after treatment, at 5 years and, for 18 patients, at 10 years, assigned patients to success or failure groups and examined variables that might predict long-term failure.[5] A clinical trial in Chinese adolescents examined the effects of maxillary protraction and its long-term stability.[12]

Wikipedia cites a 2016 randomized controlled trial in the Journal of Orthodontics (Mandall and colleagues) on early Class III protraction facemask treatment, whose title states that it reduces the need for orthognathic surgery.[1] Wikipedia's headgear article reports that long-term studies suggest facemask treatment may flatten the face and restrain chin growth, with reduced SNA and ANB angles, which are measures of the forward position of the jaws.[10]

Case series with intermaxillary elastics anchored to miniplates in children aged 10 to 13 aimed to achieve skeletal changes with fewer unwanted dentoalveolar effects; a 2010 series of six patients tested whether a temporary anchorage device could do so.[4] Ex-vivo work has studied sutural deformation during bone-anchored protraction compared with reverse-pull headgear.[13]

A 2025 systematic review in the Journal of Orthodontic Science synthesized four quantitative and four qualitative studies of bone-anchored protraction in children under 12 (116 patients in the quantitative studies), reporting improved SNA, ANB and Wits measures, stable upper incisor inclination and improved soft-tissue midface projection, and called for long-term studies.[7] A 2026 meta-analysis in Clinical and Experimental Dental Research pooled five prospective trials with 194 participants and found a mean SNA difference of 0.65 degrees in favor of skeletal anchorage over the conventional facemask, with fewer dental side effects; the authors described the skeletal gain as statistically significant but not clinically relevant and rated certainty as very low to moderate.[7]

When growth is complete, the orthodontic route for maxillary deficiency generally shifts to orthognathic surgery. Wikipedia lists jaw osteotomies, including the Le Fort I osteotomy of the upper jaw, among procedures for gross anteroposterior, vertical or transverse discrepancies, and notes that presurgical orthodontics can take up to a year.[14] Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and temporary facial numbness from nerve injury.[14] This is the evidence-based channel through which adults obtain a forward-set maxilla, as distinct from appliance pulling in growing children.

Wikipedia notes that orthodontic headgear in general is associated with tooth soreness, with younger patients feeling it within hours and adults sometimes a day later, that eye injuries have been reported (Holland and colleagues, 1985) and are reduced by safety-release straps and facebows, and that teenagers wearing visible appliances can face teasing.[10] Dentoalveolar effects and relapse after treatment are reported in the facemask literature.[4][5]

Wikipedia also records a controversy about conventional retraction headgear, which holds the upper jaw back: from the 1980s, former patients reported breathing problems and temporomandibular disorders.[10] These concerns relate to headgear that pushes the jaw backward rather than facemasks that pull it forward. For DIY pulling, a looksmax.org thread asks directly whether face pulling is bad for the temporomandibular joint, and no published study answers that question.[15]

On looksmax.org, threads on face pulling and thumb pulling discuss pulling the maxilla forward by hand or with a device in the hope of improving midface projection.[8][9] One poster in the main 'Method' thread argued that thumb pulling cannot change the face because it lasts minutes a day, whereas orthodontic headgear is worn for many hours a day for months to produce a slight change; another asked whether adult before-and-after photos exist.[8] A further thread titled as a complaint that newer members were disregarding face pulling says the site had multiple threads on it back in 2016.[9]

Other threads ask whether face pulling affects the temporomandibular joint and whether thumb-pulling results are permanent, and another is titled as showing results from a face-pulling device.[15][16][17] Face pulling sits next to other jaw and midface practices in these communities, notably mewing, an oral-posture technique that Wikipedia describes as unproven and that the American Association of Orthodontists says has no evidence of improving the jaw; Wikipedia also notes that it spread in looksmaxxing subcultures.[18] Published facemask research concerns growing children treated by orthodontists; no study of thumb pulling or of facemask use for appearance in adults was found.

Clinical studies exist in children with Class III malocclusion: cephalometric follow-ups, a clinical trial in adolescents, a randomized trial of early facemask treatment cited by Wikipedia, small case series of bone-anchored protraction, and 2025 to 2026 systematic reviews comparing skeletal and conventional anchorage.[4][5][12][1][7][7] No studies on adults using facemasks or thumb pulling for appearance were found.

lore.intro: Face pulling is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, where users describe thumb pulling or improvised headgear as a way to move the maxilla forward.[8][9]

timeline.event: Westcott reports mechanical force applied to the maxilla; Angell publishes the first paper on palatal expansion in 1860.[11]
Edward Angle's classification defines Class III malocclusion.[3]
The Haas palatal expander is reintroduced in the US.[11]
Holland and colleagues report severe eye injuries from orthodontic headgear; safety-release straps follow.[10]
Study tests the recommendation to start facemask treatment before age 8.[2]
Study of 60 Japanese children examines bone age for timing of protraction.[6]
Angle Orthodontist reports 5- and 10-year follow-up of reverse-pull headgear patients.[5]
Six-patient series tests bone-anchored protraction with miniplates and intermaxillary elastics.[4]
Clinical trial in Chinese adolescents on protraction and long-term stability.[12]
Randomized trial of early protraction facemask treatment published in the Journal of Orthodontics; looksmax.org threads on face pulling date from the same year.[1][9]
